import io
import json
import zipfile

import boto3

ROLE = "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/facilities-role"
EXPIRE_SOURCE = """
import os
import boto3


def handler(event, context):
    # A request nobody answered in time becomes EXPIRED. The condition means an already-decided request is never overwritten.
    ddb = boto3.client("dynamodb")
    try:
        ddb.update_item(TableName=os.environ["LEDGER_TABLE"], Key={"request_id": {"S": event["request_id"]}},
                        UpdateExpression="SET #s = :e", ConditionExpression="#s = :p", ExpressionAttributeNames={"#s": "status"},
                        ExpressionAttributeValues={":e": {"S": "EXPIRED"}, ":p": {"S": "PENDING"}})
        return {"expired": True}
    except ddb.exceptions.ConditionalCheckFailedException:
        return {"expired": False}
"""


def build_asl(timeout_seconds=4 * 3600):
    """The approval workflow. A human has `timeout_seconds` to answer; after that the request EXPIRES instead of waiting forever."""
    return {"Comment": "Human approval before any write", "StartAt": "RequestApproval", "States": {
        "RequestApproval": {"Type": "Task", "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke.waitForTaskToken",
                            "Parameters": {"FunctionName": "facilities-request-approval",
                                           "Payload": {"TaskToken.$": "$$.Task.Token", "request_id.$": "$.request_id",
                                                       "summary.$": "$.summary", "requester.$": "$.requester"}},
                            "ResultPath": "$.approval", "TimeoutSeconds": timeout_seconds,
                            "Catch": [{"ErrorEquals": ["States.Timeout"], "ResultPath": "$.error", "Next": "ExpireRequest"},
                                      {"ErrorEquals": ["States.ALL"], "ResultPath": "$.error", "Next": "Rejected"}], "Next": "CreateWorkOrder"},
        "CreateWorkOrder": {"Type": "Task", "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke",
                            "Parameters": {"FunctionName": "facilities-create-work-order", "Payload": {"request.$": "$"}},
                            "ResultSelector": {"work_order.$": "$.Payload"}, "ResultPath": "$.result", "End": True},
        "ExpireRequest": {"Type": "Task", "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke",
                          "Parameters": {"FunctionName": "facilities-expire-request", "Payload": {"request_id.$": "$.request_id"}},
                          "ResultPath": "$.expiry", "Next": "Expired"},
        "Expired": {"Type": "Fail", "Error": "ApprovalExpired", "Cause": "Nobody answered before the deadline"},
        "Rejected": {"Type": "Fail", "Error": "ApprovalRejected", "Cause": "Approver rejected the request"}}}


def deploy_expire_function():
    lam = boto3.client("lambda")
    buf = io.BytesIO()
    with zipfile.ZipFile(buf, "w", zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as z:
        z.writestr("expire_request.py", EXPIRE_SOURCE)
    env = lam.get_function_configuration(FunctionName="facilities-request-approval")["Environment"]["Variables"]
    try:
        lam.create_function(FunctionName="facilities-expire-request", Runtime="python3.12", Role=ROLE, Handler="expire_request.handler",
                            Code={"ZipFile": buf.getvalue()}, Timeout=30, Environment={"Variables": env})
    except lam.exceptions.ResourceConflictException:
        pass


if __name__ == "__main__":
    deploy_expire_function()
    sf = boto3.client("stepfunctions")
    arn = sf.create_state_machine(name="work-order-approval", definition=json.dumps(build_asl()), roleArn=ROLE, type="STANDARD")["stateMachineArn"]
    print("state machine", arn)

lab.title: Real approver identity and no self-approval
lab.text: A string like `duty.manager@example.com` typed into the approval proves nothing. Here the identity is the credential. The smallest form of the callback pattern (publish a task token, wait) runs with two IAM identities: the agent that asks may start the workflow but may NOT call SendTaskSuccess; the duty manager may read the inbox and answer. The audit log records which principal made each decision: that record, not a typed name, is who approved. (The simulator's STS GetCallerIdentity currently returns the account root for any key, so the audit log is the reliable record here.)

import json
import time

import boto3
from botocore.exceptions import ClientError

import iamkit
from iamkit import allow

sns, sqs, sf = boto3.client("sns"), boto3.client("sqs"), boto3.client("stepfunctions")
topic = sns.create_topic(Name="gate-topic")["TopicArn"]
qurl = sqs.create_queue(QueueName="gate-inbox")["QueueUrl"]
qarn = sqs.get_queue_attributes(QueueUrl=qurl, AttributeNames=["QueueArn"])["Attributes"]["QueueArn"]
sns.subscribe(TopicArn=topic, Protocol="sqs", Endpoint=qarn)
ASL = {"StartAt": "Ask", "States": {
    "Ask": {"Type": "Task", "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::sns:publish.waitForTaskToken", "TimeoutSeconds": 120,
            "Parameters": {"TopicArn": topic, "Message": {"request_id.$": "$.request_id", "token.$": "$$.Task.Token"}},
            "Catch": [{"ErrorEquals": ["States.Timeout"], "Next": "Expired"}, {"ErrorEquals": ["States.ALL"], "Next": "Rejected"}], "Next": "Approved"},
    "Approved": {"Type": "Succeed"}, "Expired": {"Type": "Fail", "Error": "ApprovalExpired"}, "Rejected": {"Type": "Fail", "Error": "ApprovalRejected"}}}
sm = sf.create_state_machine(name="approval-gate", definition=json.dumps(ASL), roleArn="arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/facilities-role")["stateMachineArn"]

iamkit.enforce("enforce")
agent = iamkit.principal("facilities-agent", [allow("states:StartExecution", sm), allow(["states:DescribeExecution"], "*")])
manager = iamkit.principal("duty-manager", [allow(["states:SendTaskSuccess", "states:SendTaskFailure"], "*"), allow(["sqs:ReceiveMessage", "sqs:DeleteMessage"], qarn)])

# The agent asks for approval.
ex = iamkit.client("stepfunctions", agent).start_execution(stateMachineArn=sm, name="gate-1", input=json.dumps({"request_id": "gate-1"}))["executionArn"]
msg = None
for _ in range(20):
    got = iamkit.client("sqs", manager).receive_message(QueueUrl=qurl, WaitTimeSeconds=1).get("Messages")
    if got:
        msg = json.loads(json.loads(got[0]["Body"])["Message"])
        break
assert msg and msg["request_id"] == "gate-1", "the approver must find the request in the inbox"

# 1. The agent cannot approve its own request.
since = iamkit.last_audit_id()
try:
    iamkit.client("stepfunctions", agent).send_task_success(taskToken=msg["token"], output="{}")
    raise AssertionError("self-approval must be refused")
except ClientError as e:
    assert e.response["Error"]["Code"] in ("AccessDenied", "AccessDeniedException"), e
print("agent tried to approve its own request: refused")
assert sf.describe_execution(executionArn=ex)["status"] == "RUNNING", "a refused approval must leave the request waiting"

# 2. The duty manager approves; the audit log names who.
iamkit.client("stepfunctions", manager).send_task_success(taskToken=msg["token"], output=json.dumps({"decision": "approved"}))
for _ in range(20):
    if sf.describe_execution(executionArn=ex)["status"] != "RUNNING":
        break
    time.sleep(0.25)
assert sf.describe_execution(executionArn=ex)["status"] == "SUCCEEDED"
decided = [r for r in iamkit.audit(manager, since) if r["action"] == "states:SendTaskSuccess"]
assert decided and decided[0]["decision"] == "allow", "the audit log must show who sent the approval"
refusals = [r for r in iamkit.audit(agent, since) if r["action"] == "states:SendTaskSuccess" and r["decision"] == "deny"]
assert refusals, "the audit log must also show the refused self-approval"
approver, requester = decided[0]["principal"], refusals[0]["principal"]
assert approver != requester, "separation of duties: approver and requester must differ"
print("approved by", approver, "| requested by", requester)
print("approver identity verified from the audit log")

lead: The most important rule of an agentic system: a model may propose a change, but a person approves it. This chapter makes write actions safe by parking them, recording every decision and executing only after approval.
You build an approval workflow that waits for a human, record each request in a ledger, and prove two outcomes: approve creates the work order, reject creates nothing.
concepts: Risk level
Low-risk actions can run automatically; medium and high wait for a human.
Durable wait
The workflow stores its state and a callback token, so it can wait hours or days and survive restarts.
Approval ledger
A record of every request and decision: who asked, who decided, when, with what outcome. It is the system of record.
Idempotency
Approving twice must not create two work orders. Every write carries a key that makes repeats harmless.
flow: The agent asks for a write. The request becomes a ledger row marked pending and an approver is notified.
The workflow pauses. Nothing has been written.
A human approves or rejects, sending the callback.
Approve executes the write and updates the ledger. Reject records the decision and writes nothing.
explain.example: The agent asks to open a work order for the failing air handler. It is pending. You prove no work order exists yet. You approve it, and the work order appears with the approver recorded in the ledger.
pitfalls: Executing first and asking later.
Keeping approval state in memory: a restart forgets the request.
No ledger entry on reject: you lose the record of why something did not happen.

narr.scene: The agent decides a work order is needed for the failing air handler. Priya says yes. But what if she had said no? And what if the agent had decided without asking? Nobody has built the pause yet.
narr.problem: If the agent writes first and asks afterwards, you can only apologise. And if the approval lives in memory, a restart forgets it and the request vanishes.
idea: A cheque with two signatures
Some payments need a second signer. The cheque waits, safely, until the second person signs or refuses. The workflow does that: it parks the action, durably, until a human decides.
walk: The agent asks to open a work order
The request becomes a ledger row marked pending and the approver is notified.
The workflow waits
Nothing has been written. You prove there is no work order yet.
The approver decides
They approve, sending a callback token back to the waiting workflow.
Approve creates, reject does not
Approve writes the work order and records who approved. Reject writes nothing and records why.
quiz: Why must the waiting state be durable?
For speed
A restart must not lose the request
For billing
If waiting lives in memory, the safest design fails the first time a server restarts.
Priya approves twice by accident. What prevents two work orders?
Nothing
An idempotency key on the write
A bigger server
Retries and double clicks are normal. A key makes repeating an action harmless.
A request is rejected. What should the ledger show?
Nothing
The decision, who made it and when
A deleted row
The ledger is the system of record. Knowing that something was refused, and by whom, matters as much as knowing what happened.
recap: A model proposes, a person approves, then code acts.
The wait is durable and the write is idempotent.
The ledger records every decision, including no.
narr.simple: The agent performs the write as soon as it decides to.
missing: A person deciding on real changes
A wait that survives a restart
Protection from double writes
narr.why: A model should never hold the power to change the real world on its own. Approvals also have to be provable later.
narr.design: A durable workflow parks the request, notifies the approver, records the decision in a ledger and performs the write once, with an idempotency key.

validate.what: A request is parked, not executed
validate.expect: One RUNNING execution waiting for approval
A row with status PENDING, then APPROVED or REJECTED after the decision

lab.title: Failure lab: forged, tampered and replayed tokens
lab.text: The edge is only as good as its token check. This block sends the API a valid token and then five bad ones: a token with a damaged signature, one whose payload was edited to claim an admin group, an unsigned `alg: none` token, garbage, and a token whose expiry was moved into the past. Each must be rejected before any Lambda runs; the valid token must still work. Then it hammers the API with a burst to see what the web ACL's rate rule does.
lab.code:
import base64
import json
import os
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request

import boto3

cg, ag = boto3.client("cognito-idp"), boto3.client("apigateway")
pool = next(p["Id"] for p in cg.list_user_pools(MaxResults=20)["UserPools"] if p["Name"] == "facilities-users")
cid = cg.list_user_pool_clients(UserPoolId=pool)["UserPoolClients"][0]["ClientId"]
tok = cg.initiate_auth(ClientId=cid, AuthFlow="USER_PASSWORD_AUTH",
                       AuthParameters={"USERNAME": "maria.ops@example.com", "PASSWORD": "Fac!lities-2026"})["AuthenticationResult"]["IdToken"]
api = next(a["id"] for a in ag.get_rest_apis()["items"] if a["name"] == "facilities-api")
url = os.environ["AWS_ENDPOINT_URL"].rstrip("/") + "/restapis/%s/prod/_user_request_/search" % api


def post(token):
    headers = {"Content-Type": "application/json"}
    if token is not None:
        headers["Authorization"] = token
    try:
        return urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request(url, data=b'{"query":"boiler pressure"}', method="POST", headers=headers), timeout=60).status
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
        return e.code


b64 = lambda d: base64.urlsafe_b64encode(json.dumps(d).encode()).rstrip(b"=").decode()
head, payload, sig = tok.split(".")
claims = json.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(payload + "=="))
admin = dict(claims, **{"cognito:groups": ["admin"]})
expired = dict(claims, exp=int(time.time()) - 3600)
attacks = {
    "damaged signature": ".".join([head, payload, sig[:-4] + ("AAAA" if sig[-4:] != "AAAA" else "BBBB")]),
    "payload edited to claim admin": ".".join([head, b64(admin), sig]),
    "unsigned alg:none": b64({"alg": "none", "typ": "JWT"}) + "." + payload + ".",
    "garbage": "not-a-jwt",
    "expiry moved into the past": ".".join([head, b64(expired), sig]),
}
assert post(tok) == 200, "the valid token must be accepted"
for label, bad in attacks.items():
    code = post(bad)
    assert code in (401, 403), "%s was NOT rejected (HTTP %s)" % (label, code)
    print("rejected (%d): %s" % (code, label))
assert post(None) in (401, 403)

# The rate rule from the web ACL: 100 requests per window per IP. Report what this simulator does; assert the API stays correct under load.
codes = [post(tok) for _ in range(120)]
blocked = codes.count(403) + codes.count(429)
assert set(codes) <= {200, 403, 429}, "unexpected status under load: %s" % sorted(set(codes))
print("burst of 120 valid requests: %d accepted, %d rate-limited" % (codes.count(200), blocked))
print("token attacks verified")

lead: Before anyone talks to the agent, you need to know who they are, and every layer behind the door needs to know too. This chapter builds the front door: sign-in, a verified token and a protected edge.
You create the user pool, sign a user in to get a signed token, put a firewall rule with a rate limit in front, and create an API route that rejects calls without a valid token.
concepts: Identity provider
The service that stores users and issues signed tokens after sign-in.
Token verification
The edge checks the token's signature, expiry and audience on every request. No valid token, no entry.
Identity propagation
The user's identity travels with the request through the gateway and tools, so policy and audit know the real user.
Web firewall and rate limits
Rules at the edge that block abusive traffic before it reaches your code.
flow: Create a user pool, a client and a test user.
Authenticate and receive tokens, then call the user-info endpoint with the access token.
Add a firewall with a rate-based rule.
Create the API route that needs a token and prove it refuses a call without one.
explain.example: A technician signs in and calls the search route with their token: it works. The same call without a token is rejected at the edge, so the agent behind it never sees it.
pitfalls: Verifying tokens only in the app, not at the edge.
Dropping the user identity after the first hop.
No rate limit: one client can exhaust the model budget.

narr.scene: Everything so far assumes a friendly caller. But the assistant will be on the internet. Anyone can send it a message, and the agent behind it must know whose request it is serving.
narr.problem: Without identity, every policy is guesswork. Without an edge, one noisy client can burn the whole model budget before anyone is signed in.
idea: A building's front desk
The front desk checks your badge before you reach any floor, and remembers who you are as you move around. Sign-in plus a protected edge is the front desk for the whole system.
walk: Create users
A user pool, a client and a test user for Priya.
She signs in
She receives a signed token. A call to the user-info endpoint proves it is valid.
The edge is protected

import json

import boto3

res = ask("facilities-session-" + "f" * 20)

lab.title: A cost meter and a budget limit per layer
lab.text: Cost is a feature of an enterprise agent, not an invoice surprise. Every layer gets a meter and a ceiling: tokens in and out are converted to a notional dollar figure (the simulator's models are free, the arithmetic is the lesson), published to CloudWatch with a Layer dimension, and checked against that layer's budget before the next call. The block asserts the metrics are readable per layer, an alarm exists on the budget, and a layer over budget is refused while the others keep working.
lab.code:
import boto3

import vymodels

cw = boto3.client("cloudwatch")
BUDGETS = {"model": 0.005, "search": 0.001, "memory": 0.0001}        # notional USD per run, per layer
meters = {name: vymodels.Budget(limit) for name, limit in BUDGETS.items()}


def spend(layer, kind="chat"):
    """One metered unit of work for a layer: refuse if the layer is already over budget."""
    meters[layer].check()
    if kind == "chat":
        vymodels.chat("Reply with the single word OK.")
        meters[layer].charge("chat", 120, 40)       # tokens this call used (the simulator reports real usage; fixed here so the lab is deterministic)
    else:
        vymodels.embed("boiler pressure limit")
        meters[layer].charge("embed", 400)


for layer in BUDGETS:                                                    # normal traffic
    spend(layer, "chat" if layer == "model" else "embed")
for _ in range(60):                                                      # a runaway loop in one layer only
    try:
        spend("memory", "embed")
    except vymodels.BudgetExceeded:
        break
assert meters["memory"].spent >= meters["memory"].limit, "the runaway layer must have hit its ceiling"
try:
    spend("memory", "embed")
    raise AssertionError("an over-budget layer must be refused")
except vymodels.BudgetExceeded as e:
    print("memory layer stopped:", e)
spend("model")                                                           # the other layers still work
print("model layer unaffected: %d calls, notional $%.5f of $%.4f" % (meters["model"].calls, meters["model"].spent, meters["model"].limit))

cw.put_metric_data(Namespace="FacilitiesAgent/Cost", MetricData=[
    {"MetricName": "NotionalCostUSD", "Dimensions": [{"Name": "Layer", "Value": layer}], "Value": m.spent, "Unit": "None"} for layer, m in meters.items()])
listed = cw.list_metrics(Namespace="FacilitiesAgent/Cost")["Metrics"]
layers = {d["Value"] for m in listed for d in m["Dimensions"] if d["Name"] == "Layer"}
assert layers == set(BUDGETS), "one cost series per layer expected, found %s" % sorted(layers)
for layer, limit in BUDGETS.items():
    cw.put_metric_alarm(AlarmName="budget-" + layer, Namespace="FacilitiesAgent/Cost", MetricName="NotionalCostUSD",
                        Dimensions=[{"Name": "Layer", "Value": layer}], Statistic="Maximum", Period=60, EvaluationPeriods=1,
                        Threshold=limit, ComparisonOperator="GreaterThanOrEqualToThreshold", TreatMissingData="notBreaching")
alarms = {a["AlarmName"]: a for a in cw.describe_alarms(AlarmNamePrefix="budget-")["MetricAlarms"]}
assert set(alarms) == {"budget-" + l for l in BUDGETS} and all(a["Threshold"] == BUDGETS[a["AlarmName"][7:]] for a in alarms.values())
print("cost series per layer:", sorted(layers), "| budget alarms:", sorted(alarms))
print("cost control verified")

lab.code:
import json

import boto3

kms, s3 = boto3.client("kms"), boto3.client("s3")
key = kms.create_key(Description="facilities ledger key")["KeyMetadata"]["KeyId"]
kms.create_alias(AliasName="alias/facilities-ledger", TargetKeyId=key)
kms.enable_key_rotation(KeyId=key)
assert kms.get_key_rotation_status(KeyId=key)["KeyRotationEnabled"], "rotation must be on"
print("key", key, "with alias and rotation: True")

# The record says WHAT was approved. WHO approved is not typed in: it comes from the audit trail (below), so it cannot be forged by the writer.
record = {"work_order": "WO-000104", "request_id": "req-demo-0001", "decision": "approved"}
blob = kms.encrypt(KeyId=key, Plaintext=json.dumps(record).encode(), EncryptionContext={"table": "approval-ledger"})["CiphertextBlob"]
assert b"WO-000104" not in blob, "the ciphertext must not contain the plaintext"
print("ciphertext hides the work order:", True)
back = json.loads(kms.decrypt(CiphertextBlob=blob, EncryptionContext={"table": "approval-ledger"})["Plaintext"])
assert back == record
print("decrypt with the right context:", back["work_order"])
try:
    kms.decrypt(CiphertextBlob=blob, EncryptionContext={"table": "wrong"})
    raise AssertionError("a wrong encryption context was accepted")
except kms.exceptions.InvalidCiphertextException:
    print("wrong context refused")

# Encrypt at rest by DEFAULT: every object written to the bucket is protected with the key, with no per-request flag a developer can forget.
# (This simulator reflects the bucket-default configuration; a per-request ServerSideEncryption header is accepted but reported as AES256.)
s3.put_bucket_encryption(Bucket="facilities-docs", ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration={"Rules": [
    {"ApplyServerSideEncryptionByDefault": {"SSEAlgorithm": "aws:kms", "KMSMasterKeyID": key}, "BucketKeyEnabled": True}]})
s3.put_object(Bucket="facilities-docs", Key="audit/approval-record.json", Body=json.dumps(record).encode())
head = s3.head_object(Bucket="facilities-docs", Key="audit/approval-record.json")
assert head.get("ServerSideEncryption") == "aws:kms" and key in head.get("SSEKMSKeyId", ""), "the object must inherit SSE-KMS from the bucket, got %s" % head.get("ServerSideEncryption")

lab.title: Rotate the key and prove old data still opens
lab.text: Rotation must never strand data. This block rotates the key on demand, checks the rotation was recorded, then asserts the record encrypted before the rotation still decrypts and a record encrypted after it does too. The policy lesson: rotate on a schedule, never delete old key material while ciphertext depends on it.
lab.code:
import boto3

kms = boto3.client("kms")
key = kms.describe_key(KeyId="alias/facilities-ledger")["KeyMetadata"]["KeyId"]
ctx = {"table": "approval-ledger"}
before = kms.encrypt(KeyId=key, Plaintext=b"approved before rotation", EncryptionContext=ctx)["CiphertextBlob"]
n = len(kms.list_key_rotations(KeyId=key)["Rotations"])
kms.rotate_key_on_demand(KeyId=key)
rotations = kms.list_key_rotations(KeyId=key)["Rotations"]
assert len(rotations) == n + 1, "the rotation was not recorded"
after = kms.encrypt(KeyId=key, Plaintext=b"approved after rotation", EncryptionContext=ctx)["CiphertextBlob"]
assert kms.decrypt(CiphertextBlob=before, EncryptionContext=ctx)["Plaintext"] == b"approved before rotation", "pre-rotation data became unreadable"
assert kms.decrypt(CiphertextBlob=after, EncryptionContext=ctx)["Plaintext"] == b"approved after rotation"
assert kms.get_key_rotation_status(KeyId=key)["KeyRotationEnabled"], "automatic rotation must stay on"
print("rotations recorded:", len(rotations), "| old ciphertext still opens | new ciphertext opens | automatic rotation on")
print("key rotation verified")

lab.title: Make the audit trail tamper-evident
lab.text: A trail the writer can edit is not evidence. Every ledger decision is chained: each entry's hash covers the previous hash, so changing, removing or reordering any entry breaks every hash after it. The head hash is signed with a KMS HMAC key held by a different identity than the writer, so even rewriting the whole chain is detected. The block then attacks its own trail three ways (edit an entry, delete the last entry, rewrite the chain) and asserts each is caught and located.
lab.code:
import hashlib
import json

import boto3

ddb, kms, s3 = boto3.client("dynamodb"), boto3.client("kms"), boto3.client("s3")
rows = [{k: list(v.values())[0] for k, v in i.items() if k != "task_token"} for i in ddb.scan(TableName="approval-ledger")["Items"]]
rows.sort(key=lambda r: (r.get("ts", "0"), r["request_id"]))
if len(rows) < 2:
    raise SystemExit("missing prerequisite: the ledger needs at least two decisions (run chapter 5: approve.py, reject.py)")


def chain(entries):
    out, prev = [], "0" * 64
    for e in entries:
        body = json.dumps(e, sort_keys=True)
        prev = hashlib.sha256((prev + body).encode()).hexdigest()
        out.append({"entry": e, "hash": prev})
    return out


def first_break(links):
    """Index of the first entry whose hash does not follow from the entries before it, or None."""
    prev = "0" * 64
    for i, l in enumerate(links):
        prev = hashlib.sha256((prev + json.dumps(l["entry"], sort_keys=True)).encode()).hexdigest()
        if prev != l["hash"]:
            return i
    return None


try:
    mac_key = kms.describe_key(KeyId="alias/audit-anchor")["KeyMetadata"]["KeyId"]
except kms.exceptions.NotFoundException:
    mac_key = kms.create_key(KeySpec="HMAC_256", KeyUsage="GENERATE_VERIFY_MAC", Description="signs the audit chain head")["KeyMetadata"]["KeyId"]
    kms.create_alias(AliasName="alias/audit-anchor", TargetKeyId=mac_key)


def anchor(links):
    return kms.generate_mac(KeyId=mac_key, Message=links[-1]["hash"].encode(), MacAlgorithm="HMAC_SHA_256")["Mac"]


def anchor_ok(links, mac):
    try:
        return kms.verify_mac(KeyId=mac_key, Message=links[-1]["hash"].encode(), MacAlgorithm="HMAC_SHA_256", Mac=mac)["MacValid"]
    except Exception:
        return False


links = chain(rows)
mac = anchor(links)
s3.put_object(Bucket="facilities-docs", Key="audit/chain.json", Body=json.dumps(links).encode())
assert first_break(links) is None and anchor_ok(links, mac)
print("chain of", len(links), "decisions written and signed; verifies clean")

# Attack 1: edit one entry in the middle.
t = json.loads(json.dumps(links))
t[0]["entry"]["status"] = "EXECUTED" if t[0]["entry"].get("status") != "EXECUTED" else "REJECTED"
assert first_break(t) == 0, "an edited entry must break the chain at that entry"
print("edit entry 0: chain breaks at index", first_break(t))

# Attack 2: delete the newest entry (the chain still looks internally valid, the signed head no longer matches).
t = json.loads(json.dumps(links))[:-1]
assert first_break(t) is None and not anchor_ok(t, mac), "a truncated chain must fail the signed anchor"
print("delete the last entry: hashes still chain, signed anchor rejects it")

# Attack 3: rewrite the whole chain after editing (the attacker can recompute hashes but cannot sign).
t = json.loads(json.dumps(links))
t[-1]["entry"]["status"] = "FORGED"
forged = chain([l["entry"] for l in t])
assert first_break(forged) is None and not anchor_ok(forged, mac), "a recomputed chain must fail the signed anchor"
print("rewrite the chain: hashes recompute, signed anchor rejects it")
print("tamper evidence verified")
lab.nano_note: Not verified on Nano: needs KMS GenerateMac/VerifyMac and the approval ledger populated by the Lambda-backed chapter 5.

lab.title: Who did what: the identity behind each approval
lab.text: Joins the two audit sources that chapter 5 produced: the ledger (what was decided) and the IAM audit log (which principal was allowed or refused). It asserts the approver and the requester are different identities, that the refused self-approval is on record, and says plainly which prerequisite is missing if the Enforce step was skipped.

import iamkit

recs = iamkit._admin("GET", "/api/iam/aws/audit?limit=500")["records"]
sends = [r for r in recs if r["action"] == "states:SendTaskSuccess"]
allowed = [r for r in sends if r["decision"] == "allow" and "duty-manager" in r["principal"]]
refused = [r for r in sends if r["decision"] == "deny" and "facilities-agent" in r["principal"]]

    raise SystemExit("missing prerequisite: run chapter 5 'Real approver identity and no self-approval' first "
                     "(found %d approvals by the duty manager and %d refused self-approvals)" % (len(allowed), len(refused)))

print("refused     :", requester, "tried to approve its own request at", refused[-1]["time"])
denials = [r for r in recs if r["decision"] == "deny"]

lab.title: Ship it: export the stack as Terraform, read the real-cloud warnings, rebuild and compare
lab.text: The stack you built is only worth selling if it can leave the simulator. Infrastructure Studio (in the AWS console: `#/tfstudio`) reads the live stack through the same API calls Terraform's provider makes and writes it as Terraform. This block does what a reviewer would do: export for the simulator and for a real account, read the portability warnings, fix what the warnings flag (the account id baked into the least-privilege policies from the earlier chapters), delete a table to simulate a lost environment, let Terraform plan and apply to rebuild it, and compare before and after. It also lists what the export does NOT cover, so nobody ships a stack believing the diagram is complete.
lab.code:
import json
import os
import re
import urllib.request

import boto3

EP = os.environ["AWS_ENDPOINT_URL"].rstrip("/")


def http(method, path, body=None):
    req = urllib.request.Request(EP + path, method=method, data=json.dumps(body).encode() if body is not None else None, headers={"content-type": "application/json"})
    return json.loads(urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=300).read())


sim = http("GET", "/api/terraform/export/bundle?format=json&mode=sim")
real = http("GET", "/api/terraform/export/bundle?format=json&mode=real")
have = sim["summary"]["by_type"]
print("exported", sim["summary"]["resources"], "resources:", ", ".join("%s x%d" % (k.replace("aws_", ""), v) for k, v in sorted(have.items())))
for need, n in (("aws_dynamodb_table", 3), ("aws_lambda_function", 3), ("aws_sfn_state_machine", 1), ("aws_kms_key", 1), ("aws_sns_topic", 1), ("aws_sqs_queue", 1)):
    assert have.get(need, 0) >= n, "the export is missing %s (found %d)" % (need, have.get(need, 0))

# 1. Read the warnings the export gives for a real account.
print("warnings for a real account:")
for w in real["portability"]:
    print("  [%s] %s %s" % (w["severity"], w["code"], w.get("resource", "")))
codes = {w["code"] for w in real["portability"]}
assert "unique-name" in codes, "S3 bucket names are global: the export must warn about it"

# 2. The error that matters: literal simulator account ids left inside policies the earlier chapters wrote.
literal = [(f, i + 1) for f, t in real["files"].items() for i, line in enumerate(t.split("\n")) if "123456789012" in line]
assert literal and any(w["severity"] == "error" for w in real["portability"]), "the literal account id in the least-privilege policies must be flagged as an error"
print("literal simulator account id found at:", ", ".join("%s:%d" % x for x in literal[:5]), "(%d places)" % len(literal))
for f, t in real["files"].items():
    real["files"][f] = t.replace("123456789012", "${data.aws_caller_identity.current.account_id}") if "123456789012" in t and f != "versions.tf" else t
if 'data "aws_caller_identity"' not in "\n".join(real["files"].values()):
    real["files"]["data.tf"] = real["files"].get("data.tf", "") + '\ndata "aws_caller_identity" "current" {}\n'
assert not any("123456789012" in t for t in real["files"].values()), "the account id must be parameterised everywhere"
print("fixed: the account id now comes from data.aws_caller_identity, so the same files apply in any account")
os.makedirs("terraform-export", exist_ok=True)
for name, text in real["files"].items():
    open(os.path.join("terraform-export", name), "w").write(text)
print("wrote", len(real["files"]), "files to ./terraform-export (review them; on a real account run `tofu init && tofu plan`, never apply blind)")

# 3. Re-import into the simulator: the exported files must describe exactly what is running.
bundle = {"files": sim["files"], "binaries": sim["binaries"]}
plan = http("POST", "/api/terraform/plan", bundle)
assert plan["ok"] and not plan["errors"], plan["errors"]
changes = [i for i in plan["items"] if i["action"] != "exists"]
assert not changes, "a fresh export must plan to no changes, but: %s" % [(i["address"], i["action"]) for i in changes]
print("re-import plan: %d resources, 0 changes (the files match the running stack)" % len(plan["items"]))

# 4. Lose an environment, rebuild it from the files, compare.
ddb = boto3.client("dynamodb")
before = ddb.describe_table(TableName="facilities-assets")["Table"]["KeySchema"]
ddb.delete_table(TableName="facilities-assets")
plan = http("POST", "/api/terraform/plan", bundle)
create = [i["address"] for i in plan["items"] if i["action"] == "create"]
assert create == ["aws_dynamodb_table.facilities_assets"], "exactly the deleted table must be planned for creation, got %s" % create
http("POST", "/api/terraform/apply", bundle)
after = ddb.describe_table(TableName="facilities-assets")["Table"]["KeySchema"]
assert after == before, "the rebuilt table must have the same key schema"
plan = http("POST", "/api/terraform/plan", bundle)
assert all(i["action"] == "exists" for i in plan["items"]), "after the rebuild everything must exist again"
rows = ddb.scan(TableName="facilities-assets")["Count"]
assert rows == 0, "Terraform rebuilds infrastructure, not data"
print("rebuilt facilities-assets from the files: same key schema, plan is clean again; data rows restored:", rows, "(restore data from a backup, not from Terraform)")

# 5. What the export does not cover: say it out loud.
uncovered = {}
bd, ac = boto3.client("bedrock"), boto3.client("bedrock-agentcore-control")
for label, call in (("Bedrock guardrails", lambda: bd.list_guardrails()["guardrails"]),
                    ("AgentCore gateways", lambda: ac.list_gateways()["items"]),
                    ("AgentCore memories", lambda: ac.list_memories()["memories"]),
                    ("AgentCore runtimes", lambda: ac.list_agent_runtimes()["agentRuntimes"]),
                    ("Bedrock knowledge bases", lambda: boto3.client("bedrock-agent").list_knowledge_bases()["knowledgeBaseSummaries"])):
    try:
        n = len(call())
    except Exception:
        n = 0
    if n:
        uncovered[label] = n
exported_types = set(have)
assert not {"aws_bedrock_guardrail", "aws_bedrockagent_knowledge_base"} & exported_types, "unexpected coverage claim"
print("NOT in the Terraform export (rebuild with the chapter scripts or add as your own modules):", uncovered or "nothing found")
print("ship-it verified")

lead: The last layer protects the whole application and proves what it did. Sensitive records are encrypted with keys you control, and an audit trail records who did what, so you can answer an auditor.
You create a key with rotation, encrypt and decrypt the approval record with an encryption context, store an object with server-side encryption, and read the audit trail of the run.
concepts: Envelope protection
Data is encrypted with a data key; the data key is encrypted with a master key that never leaves the key service.
Encryption context
Extra data bound to the ciphertext. Decrypting with the wrong context fails, so a record cannot be moved to another purpose.
Key rotation
Keys are replaced on a schedule without breaking old data.
Audit trail
An immutable record of control-plane and approval events: who, what and when.
flow: Create a key with an alias and turn on rotation.
Encrypt the approval record with a context; decrypt it and prove a wrong context fails.
Write an object that the storage service encrypts with the key.
Create the trail and look up the approval events from your run.
explain.example: The approval record for work order WO-17 is stored encrypted. An auditor asks who approved it: the audit trail shows the approver and the time, and the record only decrypts with the right context.
pitfalls: One key for everything.
Skipping the encryption context.
Audit logs that the same people can edit.

narr.scene: Months later an auditor asks: "Who approved work order 17, and could anyone have altered that record?" This is the question the whole course has been quietly preparing for.
narr.problem: Sensitive records stored in plain text are one breach from a headline. And without a trustworthy trail, "we are fairly sure" is the best answer you can give.
idea: A safe-deposit box with a sign-in book
The box protects what is inside. The sign-in book proves who opened it and when. Encryption protects the record; the audit trail proves what happened.
walk: Create a key
A managed key with an alias and automatic rotation.
Encrypt the approval record
With an encryption context naming the purpose. Decrypting with the wrong context fails.
Store it encrypted
The object store encrypts it with the key on write.
Read the trail
The audit log shows the approval events from your run: who, what, when.
quiz: What does an encryption context add?
Speed
A binding between ciphertext and its purpose
A copy of the key
Decrypting with a different context fails, so a record cannot be quietly reused somewhere it should not be.
Why rotate keys?
Decoration
Limit exposure over time without breaking old data
Reduce cost
Rotation shortens the window in which any one key matters.
What makes an audit trail trustworthy?
It is long
The people it records cannot edit it
It is pretty
A trail that can be edited by those it watches is a diary, not evidence.
recap: Encrypt sensitive records with a context.
Rotate keys.
An audit trail only counts if it cannot be edited by those it watches.

missing: Encryption tied to its purpose
Key rotation
A trail the people it records cannot edit

narr.design: Managed keys with an encryption context, an encrypted store and an audit log of the approval events.
